title: Vodka vs Tequila Hangover: Which Is Worse and Why?
excerpt: Is vodka or tequila better for hangovers? How congeners, methanol, 100% agave vs mixto, shots, and mixers change how you feel the next morning.
metaDescription: Vodka vs tequila hangover: which is worse? How congeners, 100% agave vs mixto tequila, shots, and mixers affect how you feel the next morning.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** drink for drink, a good vodka probably gives you a slightly milder hangover than tequila, because vodka is one of the "cleanest" spirits you can buy. It has very few of the by-products, called congeners, that seem to make hangovers worse. But the gap is small next to the things that matter far more: how much you drink, how fast you drink it, and what you mix it with. A night of four slow vodka sodas will usually feel better the next day than a night of six fast tequila shots. And a 100% agave tequila sipped over dinner can leave you feeling better than cheap vodka mixed with sugary energy drinks.

**The quick rules:** If you want the lowest-congener option, choose vodka or a 100% agave blanco tequila, not a "mixto" tequila or a dark aged spirit. Skip the rapid-fire shots, because speed drives your peak blood alcohol more than the bottle does. Choose a simple mixer like soda water over sugary or caffeinated ones. Drink water between rounds, eat before you start, and set a drink limit before you go out. No choice of liquor makes a large amount of alcohol hangover-free.

> **When to get help.** A hangover is miserable but passes on its own, usually within a day. Shots make it easy to drink more than you realize before it hits. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** can't be woken, is confused or unresponsive, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or long pauses), has a seizure, or has blue-tinged or cold, clammy skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone. **See a doctor if** your hangovers come with chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, vomiting you can't stop, or symptoms that last well beyond a day. And if you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you *stop* drinking after several days of heavy use, that's worth raising with a doctor too, since it can be a sign your body has adapted to alcohol.

## Vodka vs Tequila Hangover: The Short Comparison

Here's how the two spirits stack up on the factors that affect how you feel the next morning.

| Factor | Vodka | Tequila (100% agave blanco) | Tequila (mixto) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Congener level | Very low | Low to moderate | Moderate, plus additives |
| Methanol | Very low | Higher than vodka (comes from the agave plant) | Higher than vodka |
| Typical ABV | About 40% | About 40% | About 40% |
| Usual way it's drunk | Mixed drinks, sometimes shots | Shots, margaritas, sipped neat | Shots, cheap margaritas |
| Common hangover trap | Sugary or energy-drink mixers that hide how much you've had | Shots, which push blood alcohol up fast | Shots plus sweet mixers plus extra additives |
| Hangover verdict | Usually the mildest per drink | Close to vodka when it's good quality | Usually worse than both |

The pattern is simple. Vodka has a small head start on chemistry. Good tequila closes most of that gap. Cheap tequila widens it. And the way each one usually gets drunk can wipe out any difference in the bottle.

## What Actually Causes a Hangover

Before deciding between the two, it helps to know what you're up against. Researchers still don't fully understand hangovers, but the main drivers are fairly well agreed on:

- **The alcohol itself (ethanol).** This is the biggest factor by far. Your liver breaks ethanol down into a toxic compound called acetaldehyde, then into harmless acetate. While acetaldehyde is around, it contributes to nausea, flushing, and headache.
- **Dehydration.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. That's why you pee more when you drink, and why you wake up thirsty with a dry mouth and headache. Our guide to [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers this in more detail.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night. A lot of the next-day fog is simply bad rest.
- **Inflammation.** Studies have found that hangovers are linked to a short-term rise in inflammatory signals in the body, which may explain the achy, flu-like feeling.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which adds to nausea.
- **Congeners.** These are the extra compounds produced during fermentation, distillation, and aging. They give drinks their flavor and color, and they seem to make hangovers somewhat worse.

Notice that only the last item depends on which spirit you choose. Everything else is driven by how much ethanol you drink and how quickly. That's the key to the whole vodka vs tequila question.

## Congeners: Why Vodka Has a Head Start

Congeners are the main scientific reason people say some drinks cause worse hangovers than others. They include methanol, other alcohols (sometimes called fusel oils), acetone, acetaldehyde, esters, and tannins. Our full explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper, but here's what matters for this comparison.

### Vodka is built to remove them

Vodka is a neutral spirit. It's distilled to a very high strength, often several times, and usually filtered, then diluted with water. The goal is to strip out flavor, and flavor is largely congeners. That makes vodka one of the lowest-congener drinks available, which is why it sits at the "mild" end of almost every hangover ranking.

The best-known evidence comes from a study at Brown University published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010. Researchers gave young adults either bourbon (a high-congener spirit) or vodka (a low-congener spirit) to a fairly high blood alcohol level, then measured how they felt the next morning. People reported worse hangovers after the bourbon. But their next-day performance on attention and reaction-time tasks was impaired about equally after both drinks. In other words, the lower-congener drink felt a little better, but it didn't protect them from the effects of the alcohol itself.

Older research from the 1970s, often cited in hangover reviews, ranked drinks by how bad the hangovers were and placed brandy and dark drinks near the top and vodka at the bottom. The ranking lines up with congener content.

### Tequila sits in the middle

Tequila is made from the cooked, fermented, and distilled sugars of the blue Weber agave plant. It's distilled to a lower strength than vodka and keeps more of its raw-material character. That's why it tastes like agave and vodka tastes like almost nothing.

Unaged tequila (blanco, also called silver or plata) has fewer congeners than whiskey, rum, or brandy, but more than vodka. Aged tequilas (reposado and añejo) pick up additional compounds from the oak barrels, so they carry more congeners than blanco.

### The methanol question

One congener deserves special mention. Agave is rich in pectin, and when agave is cooked and fermented, some of that pectin breaks down into methanol. As a result, agave spirits naturally contain more methanol than vodka. Mexico's official tequila standard sets a legal ceiling on how much methanol tequila can contain, and properly made tequila stays within it.

Methanol may play a small role in hangovers. Your body breaks it down into formaldehyde and formic acid, which are toxic. In normal drinks, though, the amounts are small, and ethanol itself slows methanol breakdown while it's in your system. Some researchers think this delayed processing could contribute to the next-day feeling as the ethanol clears. It's an interesting idea but not settled. What is clear is that the methanol in legally made tequila is nowhere near the levels seen in dangerous bootleg alcohol.

## Not All Tequila Is Equal: 100% Agave vs Mixto

This is the single biggest factor in whether tequila beats or loses to vodka.

Under Mexican rules, a spirit only needs to get **51% of its sugars from blue agave** to be called tequila. The rest can come from other sugars, such as cane sugar or corn syrup. This category is called **mixto**. Mixto tequilas can also contain small amounts of permitted additives, such as caramel color, glycerin, oak extract, and sugar-based syrup, which are used to smooth or adjust the flavor and color.

Tequila made only from agave sugars is labeled **"100% agave"** or **"100% de agave"**. If a bottle doesn't say that, it's a mixto.

Why does this matter for hangovers? There aren't controlled trials comparing the hangovers from 100% agave tequila and mixto tequila directly, so be careful with anyone who quotes you exact percentages. But the reasoning is sensible:

- Mixtos are usually cheaper and made to a lower standard, which can mean a less refined distillation.
- Cheaper mixtos are the tequila of choice for fast shots and sugary margarita mixes, so they tend to be drunk in exactly the way that causes the worst hangovers.
- The "gold" color in many cheap tequilas often comes from added caramel, not barrel aging.

So when people say "tequila gives me the worst hangovers," they're often remembering a night of cheap mixto shots. That's not a fair comparison with a vodka soda. For a deeper look at tequila specifically, see our guide to [the truth about tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) and our picks for the [best tequila for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-tequila-for-no-hangover).

## Is Vodka or Tequila Better for Hangovers?

If you control for amount and speed, **vodka has a slight edge**, and **100% agave blanco tequila is a close second**. Here's how they rank, from usually mildest to usually worst, for the same number of drinks drunk the same way:

1. **Premium vodka** (very low congeners)
2. **100% agave blanco tequila** (low congeners, some methanol)
3. **100% agave reposado or añejo tequila** (more congeners from oak aging)
4. **Mixto tequila**, especially "gold" (more congeners plus additives)

The honest catch is that individual reactions vary a lot. Some people swear tequila treats them better than any other spirit. Others can't touch it. Part of that may be real chemistry, part of it may be memory of one awful night, and part may be how and where each drink was consumed. If one spirit reliably leaves you worse off, that's useful personal data, even if the general research points the other way.

For more on vodka specifically, our [vodka hangover guide](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why even "clean" vodka can still leave you rough.

## Does Tequila Give You a Worse Hangover Than Vodka?

Usually, yes, but mostly for reasons that have little to do with the spirit.

Think about how each drink tends to show up on a night out:

- **Tequila** often arrives as a round of shots, sometimes several in a row. It also comes in margaritas made with sweet pre-made mix, and those can be large drinks with more than one shot in them.
- **Vodka** often arrives in a highball: vodka soda, vodka tonic, vodka cranberry. These are sipped over 20 minutes or more, with lots of liquid alongside.

The first pattern raises your blood alcohol quickly. The second spreads it out. That difference in speed and volume is often bigger than the difference in congeners. So tequila's bad reputation is partly earned by its habits, not just its chemistry.

If you drank vodka the way people often drink tequila, in a rapid run of shots, you'd likely have a rough morning too.

## Tequila Shots vs Vodka Shots

Shot for shot, a standard 1.5-ounce pour of 40% ABV vodka and the same pour of 40% tequila contain the same amount of alcohol. Each one counts as one standard drink in the US.

What changes the outcome is pace. Here's why shots in general are hard on you:

- **They hit fast.** A shot goes down in seconds, so the alcohol reaches your bloodstream quickly. Several in a short window can push your blood alcohol much higher than the same drinks spread over a couple of hours.
- **The effect lags behind the drinking.** It can take 30 to 90 minutes for a drink to reach its full effect. Shots taken close together keep stacking before you feel the first one, which is how people end up far drunker than they planned.
- **They come in rounds.** Group shots don't follow your pace. They follow the group's.
- **They're often taken on an empty stomach.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Shots before dinner or late at night skip that buffer.

The classic tequila shot ritual of salt and lime doesn't change any of this. The salt and lime soften the taste but have no effect on the hangover.

If you want shots to cost you less the next day, the advice is the same for both spirits: fewer of them, more time between them, a full glass of water after each, and never on an empty stomach.

## Mixers Can Matter More Than the Spirit

Both vodka and tequila are mostly drunk mixed, and the mixer can change your night more than the base spirit does.

- **Sugary mixers** (sodas, juice blends, pre-made margarita mix, sweet cocktail syrups) make drinks easy to gulp, so you drink faster. They also add a lot of sugar, and many people feel worse the next day after a night of very sweet drinks.
- **Energy drinks** are a common partner for vodka. The caffeine can make you feel less drunk than you are, which tends to lead to more drinking. Health authorities have warned against mixing alcohol and energy drinks for this reason. Caffeine late at night also makes the poor sleep from alcohol worse.
- **Carbonated mixers** may speed up alcohol absorption for some people, which is one reason fizzy drinks can feel like they "go to your head" faster.
- **Simple mixers** such as soda water with fresh lime are the easiest on you. They add volume and water without extra sugar or caffeine.

A tequila soda with fresh lime (sometimes called a ranch water) and a vodka soda are roughly as hangover-friendly as mixed drinks get. Our guide to the [best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) goes through the options.

## Myths About Vodka and Tequila

A few popular claims come up again and again. Here's where they stand.

**"Tequila is an upper, not a downer."** There is no good evidence for this. Tequila is ethanol, like every other spirit, and ethanol is a depressant. People may feel more energetic on tequila because of the setting (shots, dancing, celebration) and because fast drinking produces a quick buzz before the sedating effects arrive.

**"Tequila is healthy because agave contains a special fiber."** The agave plant does contain a type of sugar fiber called agavins, and there's been some interesting early research on it. But distillation converts and separates those sugars, so a shot of tequila doesn't deliver them in any meaningful amount.

**"Expensive vodka won't give you a hangover."** Better vodka may have marginally fewer impurities, but once a vodka is properly distilled, the remaining difference is small. Price doesn't change the ethanol, and the ethanol drives most of the hangover.

**"Clear liquor never gives you a hangover."** Clear spirits tend to cause milder hangovers than dark ones for the same amount of alcohol, but they absolutely can give you a hangover. The Brown University study above showed that people still had hangovers and impaired performance after vodka.

**"Mixing vodka and tequila in one night makes it worse."** Switching drinks doesn't seem to matter much on its own. What matters is the total amount of alcohol. Nights where people mix drinks are often just nights where they drink more. Our post on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) looks at the research on drink order.

## Which Is "Healthier," Vodka or Tequila?

Neither is a health drink. Calorie for calorie and drink for drink, they're very similar. A 1.5-ounce shot of either at 40% ABV has roughly 95 to 100 calories, with essentially no carbohydrates, sugar, or fat on its own. The calories in a cocktail come mostly from the mixer.

From a hangover point of view, vodka has fewer congeners, and 100% agave tequila is close behind. Beyond that, any health difference between the two is too small to matter next to how much you drink. If you want to drink in a way that's kinder to your body, the levers are amount, pace, food, water, and sleep, not the label on the bottle.

## How to Drink Either One With a Smaller Hangover

Whichever spirit you choose, these habits do more for the next morning than the choice itself. For the full evidence-based list, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

1. **Eat a real meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol enters your blood.
2. **Pick quality.** Choose a well-made vodka or a tequila labeled "100% agave." Blanco has fewer congeners than reposado or añejo.
3. **Go easy on shots.** If you do take them, space them out and follow each with water.
4. **Choose a simple mixer.** Soda water and fresh citrus beat sugary mixes and energy drinks.
5. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water per drink helps with thirst and slows your pace.
6. **Set a limit before you start.** Decide on a number while you're sober, and stick to it.
7. **Stop a few hours before bed.** That gives your body time to process some of the alcohol before you sleep, which may improve sleep quality.
8. **Rehydrate before sleep and in the morning.** Water is fine. If you've been sweating or vomiting, an electrolyte drink can help. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers the options.

### If you already have the hangover

There's no cure, but you can make the day easier: drink water or an electrolyte drink, eat something bland, rest, and give it time. If you want a pain reliever, read the label carefully and be cautious, since acetaminophen and alcohol can be hard on the liver together, and ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that's already upset.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who enjoy the occasional tequila or vodka night add a supplement called **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**. It's a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain's response to alcohol. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data, so it's best thought of as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers on its own, and it does nothing to make shots or heavy drinking safe. It's a possible extra, not a substitute for drinking less and slower.

If you'd like to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- **Vodka usually wins by a small margin.** It's one of the lowest-congener drinks you can buy.
- **Good tequila is close behind.** A 100% agave blanco is a reasonable low-congener choice. Mixto and "gold" tequilas are the ones most likely to hurt.
- **How you drink matters more than what you drink.** Fast shots, sugary mixers, energy drinks, and an empty stomach will give you a worse hangover with either spirit.
- **No liquor is hangover-free.** The amount of alcohol is the biggest driver of how you feel the next day.
- **Know the emergency signs.** Confusion, being unable to wake someone, slow or irregular breathing, or vomiting while drowsy mean alcohol poisoning. Call 911.

For the bigger picture, our [ranking of drinks by hangover risk](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) puts every major drink type side by side, and our guide to [congeners](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains the by-products behind the differences. Beer drinkers can find the equivalent breakdown in our [beer hangover](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) guide, and the [beer vs liquor](/never-hungover/beer-vs-liquor-hangover) comparison covers the other common question.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is vodka or tequila better for hangovers?**

For the same amount of alcohol drunk at the same pace, vodka usually causes a slightly milder hangover because it has fewer congeners, the by-products that seem to make hangovers worse. A 100% agave blanco tequila comes close. Mixto tequilas, which can be made with up to 49% non-agave sugars and small amounts of additives, are more likely to leave you feeling worse. How much and how fast you drink matters more than either choice.

**Why does tequila give me such bad hangovers?**

Often it's the way tequila is drunk rather than the tequila itself. It's commonly taken as fast shots or in large, sugary margaritas, which push your blood alcohol up quickly. Cheap mixto tequila also carries more congeners and additives than 100% agave tequila. If you switch to a 100% agave blanco, sip it slowly or with soda water, and drink water between rounds, many people find tequila treats them much better.

**Are tequila shots worse than vodka shots?**

Shot for shot, they contain the same amount of alcohol if both are 40% ABV. Tequila has somewhat more congeners, so a tequila shot may contribute a bit more to a hangover, but the bigger issue is pace. Several shots of either spirit in a short time will raise your blood alcohol fast and make a hangover much more likely.

**Does 100% agave tequila prevent hangovers?**

No. There is no good evidence that any tequila prevents hangovers. A 100% agave tequila contains no added non-agave sugars and generally fewer additives than a mixto, which may make for a milder hangover, but the alcohol itself still causes dehydration, poor sleep, and the other effects behind a hangover.

**Is clear liquor really better for hangovers than dark liquor?**

Generally, yes, for the same amount of alcohol. Clear spirits like vodka, gin, and blanco tequila tend to have fewer congeners than dark spirits like bourbon, brandy, and dark rum. A 2010 study comparing bourbon and vodka found people reported worse hangovers after bourbon, though their next-day performance was impaired about equally after both. Clear liquor makes the hangover a little milder, not absent.

**Is tequila an upper and vodka a downer?**

No. Both are ethanol, and ethanol is a depressant. Tequila's energetic reputation probably comes from how it's drunk: fast shots at lively occasions give a quick buzz before the sedating effects kick in.

**Which has fewer calories, vodka or tequila?**

They're nearly identical. A 1.5-ounce shot of either at 40% ABV has roughly 95 to 100 calories and essentially no carbohydrates or sugar on its own. Most of the calories in a cocktail come from the mixer, so a vodka soda or tequila soda is far lighter than a sweet margarita or a vodka cranberry.

**What should I mix with vodka or tequila to avoid a hangover?**

Soda water with fresh lime or lemon is the simplest, lowest-sugar choice for either spirit. Avoid energy drinks, which can mask how drunk you are and disrupt sleep, and go easy on very sugary mixers and pre-made margarita mixes, which make drinks easy to gulp.
